comment.value:
ViDAR, Video Diffusion-Aware Reconstruction, is a method for dynamic 3D scene reconstruction from monocular videos. Video diffusion models are used to generate pseudo-multi-view supervisions for reconstruction with dynamic Gaussian Splatting. 

The work demonstrates strong improvements on the DyCheck dataset, particularly in dynamic regions, where it also proposes a valuable new evaluation protocol (dynamic region masks). Reviewers appreciated the practical impact and thorough experiments, with two reviewers upgrading their scores after rebuttal. 

Limitations include technical novelty (largely a combination of existing techniques), and high computational cost. 

Nonetheless, the paper provides a robust and useful pipeline that outperforms sensible baselines and bridges diffusion and 4D reconstruction. All reviewers agree that the rebuttal successfully addressed their concerns and that the submission makes a valuable contribution to the community, especially with promised open-sourcing. 

I recommend accepting the paper as a poster because it makes a solid and impactful contribution, agreed upon by all reviewers, though not conceptually novel enough for oral/spotlight.

### We would like to thank all the reviewers for their constructive comments. We believe our rebuttal addressed the concerns raised and significantly improved the quality of our paper. Below, we summarise the key points that were addressed:

- **Reviewer aMhC**
    
    We clarified our temporal consistency mechanism and contrasted it with CAT4D, which uses Video Diffusion. We showed video quality metrics in which our method surpasses CAT4D. We addressed concerns about the novelty of our approach, emphasising an ablation study that demonstrates the ineffectiveness of a naive diffusion pipeline. Additionally, we updated the computation time values based on current hardware.

    *The reviewer acknowledged our rebuttal as detailed and agreed that we addressed their concerns.*

- **Reviewer wqBG**
    
    We provided results from a new dataset (NVIDIA dynamic). We explored the potential to reduce the number of input views needed to fine-tune the diffusion model, showing a potential adaptability to a static, sparse view scenario. We discussed the issue of smoothed textures and attribute them to high camera pose noise in DyCheck, as we do not observe them in NVIDIA. We offered further clarification on ensuring the geometric consistency of our reconstruction.

    *Although the reviewer did not explicitly comment on the rebuttal, we believe all concerns were addressed thoroughly.*

- **Reviewer coKt**
    
    We included a new ablation study isolating the effect of the diffusion model. We provided a more detailed comparison with CAT4D, including video quality metrics to highlight the consistency of our output. We provided an experiment comparing personalised diffusion (Ours) against the general restoration model (DIFIX3D+). We addressed the question on the choice of diffusion model, code release and the title of our paper.

    *The reviewer acknowledged that our rebuttal effectively addressed their concerns and expressed confidence in the robustness of our pipeline.*

- **Reviewer wkEa**
    
    We provided a new ablation on the dependence on dynamic mask accuracy. We added more in-depth analysis on artefacts carried over from the baseline geometry. We included an experiment on in-the-wild videos and demonstrated our effectiveness through video quality metrics. We provided a detailed analysis of the possible failure modes and how they can be mitigated. 

    *The reviewer acknowledged that our rebuttal strengthened the empirical validity of our approach.*

Thank you for appreciating the contributions of ViDAR, especially in terms of performance increase in dynamic regions. We address the remaining question below.

 ### Could you summarise the most common irrecoverable vs. recoverable failure modes you observe and outline any mitigation you foresee?

 We observe two possible sources of failure modes in ViDAR. Firstly, the diffusion- and camera-sampling-induced inconsistencies, and secondly, the failures carried over from the baseline geometry - MoSca. We address them as follows:
1. Diffusion- and camera-sampling-induced inconsistencies
    - **RECOVERABLE**  
    As mentioned by the reviewer aMhC and addressed in our response, image diffusion model in itself does not produce temporarily consistent outputs.  
    *Mitigation*:  
    We apply the supervision signal for the Gaussians specifically for dynamic regions, and we resolve camera pose misalignments with additional camera optimisation. 
    - **RECOVERABLE**  
    With noisy camera poses the rendered images may not correspond to the sampled camera pose.  
    *Mitigation*:  
    We apply camera pose optimisation to the sampled camera poses based on dynamic content, which resolves the pose ambiguity.  
    - **IRRECOVERABLE**  
    Present in baseline MoSca as well, heavily underrepresented in the input video parts of the scene cannot be recovered in the reconstruction. We refer the reviewer to results_video.mp4 in our supplementary, paying particular attention to the underside of the pillow at *0:10-0:11s* - we note that it was not reconstructed correctly due to being visible only a handful of frames.  
    *Potential solutions*:  
    We believe that future research may include a two-fold approach to enriching reconstruction in underrepresented areas of the scene. Firstly, one may try to identify regions of high uncertainty and cater supervision curriculum towards such frames, generating and enhancing more samples. Further, one may include a different diffusion supervision in those areas, namely, an inpainting model, designed to hallucinate missing geometry.
2. Geometry inconsistencies carried over from MoSca:
    - **RECOVERABLE**  
    We observe presence of many small floaters on the boundary of dynamic region in MoSca.  
    *Mitigation*:  
    As added in the response to the reviewer's initial questions, we observe that the use of Track-Anything masks improves upon noisy masks obtained by thresholding the opacity of dynamic Gaussians. Notably, it is not the major improvement in the performance of ViDAR, however, we notice that qualitatively it contributes to the reduction of floaters around the boundary of dynamic regions. An example of such can be seen around the hand in *spin* scene in results_video.mp4 *1:51-1:53s*.
    - **RECOVERABLE**  
    With only one camera as an input and the only source of supervision, MoSca is prone to being heavily affected by the problem of shape-pose ambiguity. This can be observed in the *pillow* scene in results_video.mp4. Throughout the whole scene, we observe a jittering of the camera, and at *0:08-0:10s* we see the upper body detaching from the legs. 
    *Mitigation*:  
    We believe that ViDAR resolves this issue by design. In the process of camera sampling, we create a pseudo-multi-view capture. This, combined with camera pose optimisation, allows for more certainty in Gaussian positions optimisation, simply due to points being observed from more (virtual) cameras. In the aforementioned example, we observe a stable camera and a consistent geometry of the whole body. It is worth noting that *pillow* is a qualitative-only scene, without ground-truth poses, therefore, MoSca cannot perform test-time camera optimisation. This means that both methods were fed with one stationary camera pose as a rendering target, yet produced drastically different results.

As a last remark, we agree that performance is limited to a degree by baseline geometry. Therefore, we have chosen a state-of-the-art method as our baseline. Notably, we see many methods build upon previously seen backbones, and we outperform MoSca by a large margin, achieving state-of-the-art results on two major monocular reconstruction diagnostic datasets. In the future, we expect the research community to improve the monocular reconstruction quality. In such a case, we believe that our diffusion-aware enhancement and supervision will still be applicable with stronger backbones.

The added NVIDIA-dataset results, extended ablations (“w/o diffusion”, “w/o TA”) and the VBench temporal-consistency metrics convincingly show (i) a measurable gain over MoSca/CAT4D in dynamic regions and (ii) that personalised diffusion contributes ~0.35 dB PSNR / 11 % LPIPS when integrated with your diffusion-aware loss and pose optimisation. These updates solidify ViDAR’s empirical value and justify my borderline-accept stance.
Remaining concerns are chiefly conceptual: the method’s novelty lies more in a robust composition of existing blocks and its success is still gated by baseline geometry—failure patterns under heavy occlusion or severe pose error are only qualitatively described. 
Could you summarise the most common irrecoverable vs. recoverable failure modes you observe and outline any mitigation you foresee? That clarification would further sharpen the paper’s contribution.

|Ours w/o diffusion|18.65|0.660|0.408|15.54|0.884|0.435|

 

The reviewer validly highlights that Table 4 shows that removing some of the proposed techniques leads to degradation in quality that can be worse than the initial MoSca, especially *Ours w/o SO + DR + TGS*. It was our intention to show this. Attempting to naively integrate diffusion leads to degraded performance due to the view-time inconsistency of the diffusion outputs. Our novel *diffusion-aware reconstruction* is needed to incorporate 2D diffusion models into our pipeline in a view-time consistent manner, and such that they improve performance.

On the other hand, we use publicly available 2D diffusion models and aim to ensure view-time consistency at the *reconstruction* stage, instead of at the *generation* stage. From the results on the DyCheck dataset, our approach seems to yield more consistent outputs across all test scenes, as shown in the supplementary videos. *Table R4. Video consistency metrics on DyCheck dataset.*

|Method|subject consistency|background consistency|motion smoothness|aesthetic quality|imaging quality|
|-|-|-|-|-|-|
|Raw diffusion output|0.9333|0.9273|0.9630|0.4020|**0.5720**|
|MoSca|0.9375|0.9323|0.9911|0.4197|0.5535|
|CAT4D|0.9440|0.9394|0.9939|0.3962|0.5521|
|Ours|**0.9460**|**0.9439**|**0.9941**|**0.4262**|0.5588|
|*GT*|*0.9477*|*0.9489*|*0.9969*|*0.4577*|*0.7534*|

Nevertheless, our work includes a comparison to CAT4D and outperforms it in the provided metrics.

We intend to release code upon acceptance (and after internal evaluation), as well as to release dynamic masks needed for evaluating the new dynamic region benchmark for DyCheck.

Thanks to the recent code release (11/06/2025), we were able to design an experiment directly comparing the two diffusion approaches. |Method|PSNR-m|SSIM-m|LPIPS-m|PSNR-D|SSIM-D|LPIPS-D|
|-|-|-|-|-|-|-|
|MoSca|14.52|0.592|0.578|14.41|0.669|0.499|
|Ours-DIFIX3D+-NoRef|15.22|0.615|0.550|15.00|0.676|0.465|
|Ours-DIFIX3D+-Ref|15.15|0.615|0.553|14.92|0.675|0.467|
|Ours|**15.63**|**0.624**|**0.478**|**15.46**|**0.689**|**0.413**|

 

Notably, all diffusion approaches outperform MoSca. We observe that images enhanced with personalised diffusion (Ours) provide a better supervision signal in our pipeline. Nevertheless, we believe that there exists a potential use case for both approaches, and both can be used to design a reconstruction pipeline.

The core of our idea includes personalisation of diffusion and frame-by-frame reference for enhancement. To the best of our knowledge, during the design phase of ViDAR, personalisation of Video Diffusion was not yet developed. Therefore, we opted to use the image diffusion model. We believe that with the rapid development of video diffusion models, a reliable geometrical grounding will become viable, and the models will become more in line with our pipeline.

Therefore, to validate the potential of using sparse supervision, we designed a small experiment in which we replaced the diffusion model trained on the full input video with one trained on 3 or 6 frames (equally spaced in time). We note that for the examples mentioned e.g. "teddy", "block" and "space-out", although SoM and MoSca may appear to have sharper textures in places, we recommend viewing the main results video (*00:50-01:23, 01:59-02:23*), where the textures are not view-time consistent and are sometimes floating in space. Therefore, we employ several mechanisms to best use the benefits of diffusion enhancement. Firstly, we employ the supervision specifically for dynamic regions, as a monocular capture of a static region can be translated to a multi-view capture with corresponding camera poses. Secondly, we perform additional optimisation of the sampled camera poses, which resolves potentially induced misalignments. We believe this successfully mitigates the effects of training on inconsistent outputs.

# Response to Reviewer aMhC

We thank the reviewer for their positive comments and constructive feedback and address key concerns below.

 

### The computation time is slow. 
Our previously reported time-complexity figures were measured when running on a fairly dated GPU (released in 2017, with approx. 7 TFLOPS fp32). Current GPU hardware is substantially faster than that (e.g. 60 - 80 TFLOPS fp32). To prove this, we run our pipeline on a more current GPU (released in 2024, 60 TFLOPS fp32), and report an average total training time of 4 hours per scene, with 2 hours for diffusion and 2 hours for reconstruction. This is 6x faster than our previously reported times and is thus in line with other per-scene optimisation approaches.

 

### Our pipeline is a simple combination of per-scene optimisation and diffusion, novelty is constrained.
We agree that our pipeline is a combination of per-scene optimisation and a DreamBooth-adapted diffusion model; however we note that it is non-trivial to combine these components together effectively. We show in our ablation study that naively combining the two (Table 4, Ours w/o SO + DR + TGS, 18.46dB) does not lead to much improvement in PSNR compared to MoSca alone (18.44dB) due to the spatio-temporal inconsistency of diffusion outputs. Our *diffusion-aware* pipeline is novel because we demonstrate that it is possible to use inconsistent diffusion outputs to improve reconstruction quality (19.00dB) while still maintaining consistency. To our knowledge, we're the first to incorporate publicly available 2D diffusion models into 4D reconstruction of real-world monocular videos in a geometrically consistent manner. 

 

### Pseudo-GTs from SDXL/DreamBooth are not view-time consistent. Relying on these is tenuous.
We agree that the outputs of our personalised diffusion model are not view-time consistent. We show this in our supplementary video *(2:34-3:28)* and also highlight this issue in our main manuscript *(Sec 3.3 Diffusion-Aware Reconstruction)*. It is not trivial to use inconsistent supervision effectively for 4D reconstruction. However, we design our diffusion-aware reconstruction pipeline to take this *feature* of 2D diffusion models into account. The key observations in our work suggest that monocular reconstruction methods struggle with reconstructing the dynamic content due to shape-pose ambiguity, which often presents as high-frequency artefacts (e.g. supplementary *spin.mp4* - *0:02-0:03* - MoSca). To mitigate that we employ a personalised diffusion model to create a pseudo-multi-view capture of the scene. Notably, diffusion output is not perfect and fully consistent, yet it yields strong support for ambiguous geometry. Thus, we employ such a supervision signal specifically for dynamic regions, resolving potential misalignments with additional camera optimisation. We successfully mitigate the effects of training on inconsistent outputs, and we show this in our supplementary video, where our results demonstrate much greater view-time consistency than the diffusion outputs and other diffusion-based methods such as CAT4D. Additionally, we run video quality estimation on the results of our method, as well as MoSca, CAT4D and raw diffusion outputs (and ground truth as the upper bound) to quantify the temporal quality of the produced videos. We use the VBench suite (CVPR24) which offers the following metrics for non-reference quality estimation: *subject consistency*, *background consistency*, *motion smoothness*, *aesthetic quality*, *imaging quality*.

 

*Table R4. Video consistency metrics on DyCheck dataset.*

|Method|subject consistency|background consistency|motion smoothness|aesthetic quality|imaging quality|
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
|Raw diffusion output|0.9333|0.9273|0.9630|0.4020|**0.5720**|
|MoSca|0.9375|0.9323|0.9911|0.4197|0.5535|
|CAT4D|0.9440|0.9394|0.9939|0.3962|0.5521|
|Ours|**0.9460**|**0.9439**|**0.9941**|**0.4262**|0.5588|
|*GT*|*0.9477*|*0.9489*|*0.9969*|*0.4577*|*0.7534*|

 

Notably, we notice that our method provides the best performance in majority of metrics. Unsurprisingly, personalised diffusion outputs score very high in *imaging quality*, we believe due to very sharp images which are not necessarily consistent temporally.

 

### If any part of our response is unclear or raises further questions, we would greatly appreciate the opportunity to clarify during the discussion phase.

summary.value: The paper presents ViDAR, an algorithm for 4D reconstruction from monocular videos, addressing the challenge of generating high-quality novel views of dynamic scenes with spatio-temporal consistency. ViDAR employs MoSca to create a 4D scene representation and samples novel camera poses to produce degraded multi-view renderings. Leveraging a DreamBooth-adapted diffusion model, it refines these renders into pseudo-supervision signals. To resolve diffusion-induced inconsistencies, the approach incorporates a diffusion-aware loss and camera pose optimization.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
Strengths:
1. The paper features high readability and a well-structured logical flow.
2. Experiments on the DyCheck dataset demonstrate significant advantages over state-of-the-art methods.

Weaknesses:
1. The methodological novelty is constrained, resembling a combination of per-scene optimization (MoSca) and a DreamBooth-adapted diffusion model.
2. There is a lack of theoretical support or prior evidence indicating that DreamBooth or SDXL can ensure view-time consistency. Relying on such pseudo-GTs to achieve spatio-temporal consistency appears tenuous.
3. The computation is excessively time-consuming, with the diffusion enhancement stage alone taking up 12 hours.

questions.value: As noted in the Weaknesses section, a more detailed explanation of how misaligned diffusion outputs nonetheless enhance result consistency would make the proposed method far more convincing.

summary.value: This work aims to reconstruct the dynamic 3D scene from one monocular video and proposes Video Diffusion-Aware Reconstruction (ViDAR), which utilizes diffusion models to generate pseudo-multi-view supervisions for the training of the dynamic Gaussian Splatting. Specifically, this work generates fine-grained details by conditioning the scene-specific features and introduces the diffusion-aware loss function and the strategy of camera pose optimization.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
Strengths
  * The core idea of this work includes diffusion enhancement and pseudo-novel-view sampling. The proposed approach sounds like it makes sense.
  * The dynamic region mask for evaluation is valuable since the co-visibility mask metrics of the DyCheck dataset [C] are largely confounded by good reconstructions of static regions. Extended evaluation of dynamic region masks should be widely adopted.
  * This paper is well-written and is easy to understand.

* Weakness
  * Although the method proposed in this work is very easy to understand, it is difficult to tell the difference between 4D reconstruction and 3D reconstruction using the diffusion enhancement method. That is, the proposed method can also be inserted into a static 3D reconstruction setting (like sparse views, blurring, etc.). I think the key to using diffusion enhancement in 4D reconstruction is to explain how to solve the problem of how to generate content and ensure the consistency of geometric structure at the same time.
  * The rendered images of the proposed method tend to be smooth and blurred. For example, in Figure 4, the sleeve textures of "teddy", the clothes textures of "block", and the pants textures of "space-out", are compared to SoM [A] and MoSca [B]. Is this due to diffusion enhancement?
  * This work only conducts experiments on one dataset, i.e. the DyCheck dataset [C]. It is not sufficient. Meanwhile, as far as I know, there may exist pose errors in the DyCheck dataset [C] as illustrated in Appendix A.3. of MoDGS [D]. Therefore, this work should be supplemented with more quantitative results on dynamic reconstruction datasets.

[A] Wang Q, Ye V, Gao H, et al. Shape of motion: 4d reconstruction from a single video[J]. arXiv preprint arXiv:2407.13764, 2024.

[B] Lei J, Weng Y, Harley A W, et al. Mosca: Dynamic gaussian fusion from casual videos via 4d motion scaffolds[C]//Proceedings of the Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition Conference. 2025: 6165-6177.

[C] Gao H, Li R, Tulsiani S, et al. Monocular dynamic view synthesis: A reality check[J]. Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems, 2022, 35: 33768-33780.

[D] Qingming L I U, Liu Y, Wang J, et al. MoDGS: Dynamic Gaussian Splatting from Casually-captured Monocular Videos with Depth Priors[C]//The Thirteenth International Conference on Learning Representations. 2025.

summary.value: ViDAR is a 4D reconstruction framework that takes a monocular video as input. ViDAR initializes the 4D representation with a prior 4D monocular video reconstruction work, MoSca, which produces a 4D Gaussian splatting representation. Stable Diffusion XL model is finetuned to be personalized for the input monocular video such that the model captures the distribution of the images from the current video better. This personalized model is used to enhance the quality of novel view samples, which are then used together with the original video to enhance the quality of 4D Gaussians. ViDAR demonstrates superior quality over the prior 4D monocular video reconstruction approaches.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
Strengths:
- ViDAR presents a pipeline for a challenging and useful 4D monocular video reconstruction task that has a lot of downstream applications, such as simulation and content creation.  
- ViDAR outperforms previous approaches both qualitatively and quantitatively, and presents results with comparison with multiple other works. It also points out the limitations of metrics and proposes an enhanced metric that focuses more on the dynamic regions of scenes that are more relevant for the task. On top of the summary above, it further proposes techniques to enhance the quality of 4D representation, namely Tracking-based Gaussian Classification, Sampled Camera Optimization, and Dynamic Reconstruction, whose effectiveness is demonstrated.
- The paper is clearly written and easy to follow.

Weaknesses:
- The main part of the proposed pipeline is a combination of popular techniques, such as dataset enhancement with Diffusion Model works (ex. Instruct-Nerf2Nerf (Haque et al. 2023), ReconFusion (Wu et al. 2023)) and personalized DM for view reconstruction (ex. RefFusion, Mirzaei et al. 2024), on top of a strong 4D initialization given by MoSca. I believe the novelty of the work comes from the robustness of the pipeline, and the effect of each component needs to be more clearly demonstrated. 
    - Table 4 shows that removing some of the proposed techniques shows degradation in quality that can be worse than the initial MoSca. This could suggest that the personalized DM do not contribute much to the performance of the pipeline, unless more evidences are supported.
    - Compared to other state-of-the-art methods, such as CAT4D, ViDAR leverages more information such as depth map and 2D tracks. It is not clear if adding one or two proposed components to CAT4D (especially MoSca initialization) could make it perform better. Note that I do not mean that this wouldn't be okay, but it is not clear which component is adding the most benefit.
- ViDAR uses a personalized image diffusion model, but the name of the method (Video Diffusion-Aware … ) is misleading which suggests a ‘video diffusion’ model is used. In line 160, it is actually mentioned ‘a personalized video diffusion model’ - I believe this is incorrect. 

Minor:
- In line 94, CAT4D is mentioned as a concurrent work, but it appeared on Arxiv on Nov 27, 2024, which is prior to the date (March 1, 2025) NeurIPS considers as concurrent.

questions.value:
- As I believe the significance of the work comes from building a robust pipeline for 4D monocular video reconstruction, it would be great to have the code released such that the community can benefit from it. Would it be a possibility? 
- Regarding the first point in weaknesses, it would be great to have additional ablations demonstrating the effect of each component more clearly. 
  - Minor: Recent works such as DIFIX3D+ (Wu et al. 2025) suggest that training a general diffusion model for enhancement purposes might be better than a personalized model. This is concurrent work, so it is just a suggestion to include some further discussion on the benefit of personalized DM.
- Why was a video diffusion model not used, and an image diffusion model was used instead? Apart from the confusion mentioned in the weakness section, there is no clear discussion on this choice.

final_justification.value: The paper demonstrates a robust pipeline for 4D monocular video reconstruction, and the authors addressed my initial concerns with a new set of experiments. However, I believe the impact of the work, while it proposes a robust pipeline, might be limited as the work is a combination of prior techniques. Therefore, I rate the final rating as 'borderline accept'.

summary.value: The authors propose ViDAR, a monocular-video pipeline that (i) personalises an SDXL diffusion model to the target clip (DreamBooth-style), (ii) enhances renders from a monocular Gaussian-splat baseline (MoSca) to create high-fidelity pseudo-multi-view supervision, and (iii) introduces diffusion-aware reconstruction: losses that mask supervision to dynamic pixels and a joint optimisation of the sampled camera poses. On the DyCheck benchmark, ViDAR reports superior PSNR/SSIM—particularly in dynamic regions—across all 14 scenes and supplies an ablation isolating each contribution.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
Strengths:
Bridges generative diffusion priors with geometrically-consistent monocular 4D reconstruction; supplies a dynamic-mask benchmark.

Weakness:
1. Dependency on Baseline Geometry – Authors acknowledge diffusion cannot fix large geometric errors; performance is still gated by MoSca quality.
2. Ablation Scope – No study on diffusion-mask accuracy; sensitivity to Track-Anything noise is unclear.

questions.value:
Failure Modes – What artefacts remain when baseline geometry is poor (e.g., heavy occlusion)? Examples or quantitative failure analysis would be valuable.
Generalisation – Have you tried ViDAR on truly in-the-wild phone clips beyond DyCheck? Qualitative evidence would help.

limitations.value: The paper notes diffusion cannot repair major geometric errors and that training is compute-heavy.

value: NO or VERY MINOR ethics concerns only

final_justification.value:
The NVIDIA benchmark, the “w/o diffusion” ablation, and the 4 h/scene runtime quantify ViDAR’s uplift in dynamic regions. Although the approach is incremental and still bound to MoSca’s geometric prior, the model is still useful for certain cases and the authors answered my question about failure cases well. So I’m raising my score to 5 (Accept). 

I look forward to the promised open-source release of code and dynamic masks for community validation and extension.

title.value: ViDAR: Video Diffusion-Aware 4D Reconstruction From Monocular Inputs

abstract.value: Dynamic Novel View Synthesis aims to generate photorealistic views of moving subjects from arbitrary viewpoints. This task is particularly challenging when relying on monocular video, where disentangling structure from motion is ill-posed and supervision is scarce. We introduce Video Diffusion-Aware Reconstruction (ViDAR), a novel 4D reconstruction framework that leverages personalised diffusion models to synthesise a pseudo multi-view supervision signal for training a Gaussian splatting representation. By conditioning on scene-specific features, ViDAR recovers fine-grained appearance details while mitigating artefacts introduced by monocular ambiguity. To address the spatio-temporal inconsistency of diffusion-based supervision, we propose a diffusion-aware loss function and a camera pose optimisation strategy that aligns synthetic views with the underlying scene geometry. Experiments on DyCheck, a challenging benchmark with extreme viewpoint variation, show that ViDAR outperforms all state-of-the-art baselines in visual quality and geometric consistency. We further highlight ViDAR’s strong improvement over baselines on dynamic regions and provide a new benchmark to compare performance in reconstructing motion-rich parts of the scene.

reviewer_nomination.description: Every submission must nominate at least one author who is a qualified reviewer (i.e., satisfying our reviewer nomination criteria https://blog.neurips.cc/2025/03/10/self-nomination-for-reviewing-at-neurips-2025/ ). Being named as such a reviewer in the submission constitutes an acceptance and a commitment to carry out the regular reviewing load (~6 papers) responsibly if asked by the PC chairs or the D&B track chairs. Only if no qualified reviewer exists in the author list, nominate the best-qualified author for consideration by the PC chairs or the D&B track chairs. In addition, note that any author listed on 4 or more papers will be automatically regarded as a reviewer unless they are already serving as a reviewer, AC, SAC, or other roles in the Organization Committee. Failure to assign a qualified reviewer when one is available in the author list may result in desk rejection. Please enter an email address or OpenReview ID that exactly matches one of the authors (separate by comma if more than one nominations).

responsible_reviewing.description: We acknowledge that every author on the program committee is obligated to conduct responsible reviewing according to the policy designed by the PC Chairs and relevant members of the organizing committee. **Failure to do so may result in desk rejection or other serious consequences.**
